claims.claim: A portfolio is the combined holdings of investments — stock, bond, and other assets — held by an individual or institutional investor; it is the whole collection, not any single item in it.
Diversification operates at the portfolio level: spreading money among different investments to reduce risk is done within the portfolio, so no single holding decides the portfolio's outcome.
Asset allocation is the mix: dividing a portfolio's money among broad categories of assets — stocks, bonds, and cash (equities, fixed-income, and cash and equivalents).

Rebalancing is bringing a drifted portfolio back to its target mix: over time some investments grow faster than others, pushing holdings out of alignment and changing the portfolio's risk level, so the owner sells some of what grew and/or adds money to other categories.

Rebalancing works best when done relatively infrequently, whether on a regular schedule (such as every six or twelve months) or when a category drifts past a preset threshold, and it is effectively buying low and selling high.

A portfolio's risk depends on how its holdings move together: combining holdings that are not perfectly correlated reduces the portfolio's swings, because gains in one holding can offset losses in another.
A portfolio's return depends on the returns of everything inside it — the expected return of the portfolio is the blend of what its holdings return.
The asset allocation decision is personal: it changes at different times in a person's life depending on time horizon and risk tolerance, and it is influenced by personal goals.
A portfolio drifts on its own as markets move, silently changing its risk level, so it needs periodic watching and rebalancing rather than being set and forgotten.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often a portfolio should be rebalanced: Investor.gov reports that some financial experts advise regular intervals (such as every six or twelve months) while others recommend rebalancing when a category drifts more than a preset percentage.
positions: Rebalance on a fixed calendar schedule (e.g., every six or twelve months)
Rebalance when an asset class drifts beyond a preset threshold
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both approaches as the described range of practice and keeps the shared, source-supported point: rebalancing tends to work best when done relatively infrequently. No single schedule is endorsed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The word 'portfolio' is defined slightly differently across sources: Investor.gov's glossary defines it as combined holdings of stock, bond, commodity, real estate, and other investments, while OpenStax introduces it as the collection of stocks an investor owns.
positions: Portfolio as holdings across many asset types (Investor.gov)
Portfolio as a collection of stocks (OpenStax's investing context)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses Investor.gov's broader definition as the working definition and treats OpenStax's wording as the same concept in a stock-focused context. Both agree the portfolio is the collection, not a single holding.
